title: Syllabus
text:
The key components of the syllabus are outlined below. The complete syllabus (PDF) has additional policies and information about the course. Please read it carefully.

OverviewLearning GoalsMaterialGrading



Overview
For most of human history, living standards barely changed. Then, beginning around 1700, they took off, first in Britain and then across much of the world. Behind this takeoff was a new way of organizing economic life, capitalism, built on private property, markets, and firms. This course is about the nuts and bolts of how that system works.
We build the core tools of microeconomics and use them to answer everyday questions along the way: Why are almost all the big brands in the grocery store owned by ten companies? Why does Cheerios cost more than the store brand sitting right next to it, and why do people keep buying it anyway? When bird flu sent egg prices soaring, were companies profiting or just surviving? If the government taxes gasoline, who bears the burden, the oil companies or you? Is capping rent to make housing affordable a good idea? Why do we end up with more pollution than anyone actually wants? And why do some things, like parks and street cleaning, need to be provided by the government instead of businesses?




Learning Goals
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

Understand how to measure opportunity cost and apply it to determine optimal choices or trade-offs
Determine a predicted market equilibrium using information from graphs or tables describing demand and supply decisions
Calculate elasticities (own price, income, or cross-price) using price and quantity data
Understand how to measure economic surplus and apply it to determine the efficiency of trades or transactions
Use the supply and demand model to predict the equilibrium effects of government interventions in markets
Calculate marginal products and marginal costs, and use this information to determine profit-maximizing decisions
Understand the characteristics related to market structures (perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly)





Required Texts
The required textbook for this course is The Economy 2.0: Microeconomics by CORE Econ. The complete textbook is free and open access, available online at:

https://books.core-econ.org/the-economy/microeconomics

The online edition is the version I will refer to in class. If you prefer reading on paper, a printed paperback is available from the publisher (Hackett, ISBN 978-1-64792-160-6).

title: Introduction to the Course
text:
About me




Delhi


→



Boston


→



SoCal





This is my fourth year at CSUF. I also teach microeconomics in the master’s program and a 400-level math class that is open to undergraduates.
My research is in labor economics: employment and wages. Right now I am studying California’s fast-food minimum wage using large-scale job vacancy data.
If you are curious about economic research or data analysis, or you just want advice about careers or school, my office hours are open. It does not have to be about this class.
I was born and raised in Delhi, did my PhD in Boston, and moved here with my wife and our dog Dobby, a twenty-pound rat terrier.
I used to have hobbies: cooking, board games, anything outdoors. I hope to have them again. For now I have a raging toddler.
What drew me to economics: I started it in school, liked it more in my bachelor’s, then did a master’s, then a PhD. It kept getting better.
The real reason is simpler. I grew up around inequality and around systems that plainly did not work. I wanted to understand why, and I wanted to do something about it. I do not know how much I have managed to do, but I understand it far better now.
My hope is that you come to see what I saw: economics gives you an elegant framework for simplifying complicated things, and it points that framework at questions that matter.
Before we go on, I want to know something about you. Going around a room of 120 is not realistic, so let us do a quick poll if you have a phone.

Then ask the real one: why are you taking this class?
Most answers will be some version of “it is required.”
Say so out loud: that is completely fair. Most of you are here because a requirement put you here. Here is my end of the deal. My job is to make the seat time worth it, so that you leave with tools you actually use.

title: Introduction to the Course
text:
Why this class?

Economics is about choices when you cannot have everything
Microeconomics: the choices of people and firms, and the markets where they meet
Macroeconomics, for contrast: the whole economy at once
We build a small set of tools, then point them at real questions



Micro is the part where you can usually see the mechanism, which is why it comes first.
Keep the definition short. The next slide does the selling.
For business students: every one of these tools shows up in pricing, costs, and competitive strategy.

title: Introduction to the Course
text:
Questions we will answer

Why do ten companies own most grocery brands?
Why does Cheerios cost more than the store brand next to it?
When egg prices spiked, was that greed or cost?
Who really pays a gas tax, the oil company or you?
Do rent caps make housing affordable?
Why is there more pollution than anyone wants?



Read two or three of these out loud and let the room react. Do not answer them.
Point out that the same small set of tools answers all six.
Say the promise plainly: you already have opinions about these. By December you will have arguments.

title: Introduction to the Course
section: Three things I ask of you
text:
Three things I ask of you

Be here. Quizzes are almost every Monday
Be present. Phones and laptops away; tablets flat for notes
Take part. Worksheets, polls, and questions out loud


Do these three and I promise this class is more fun and much less of a drag.



On being here: I will do my best to make class worth your time. In exchange, show up. We also practice together in class most sessions. Attendance is not a separate grade, but it is the best predictor of how this course goes for you, and missing a Monday usually costs you a quiz.
On devices: randomised trials at West Point found that in-class computer use lowered exam scores, including for the students sitting near the laptop. It is not about trust.
On taking part: explaining your reasoning to the person next to you is where the ideas stick. Worksheets are never collected or graded, so mistakes in class are free.
Asking a question in a room of 120 is a favour to everyone too shy to ask it.

title: Introduction to the Course
text:
How to succeed

Keep up with the reading as it is assigned
Do each week’s practice problems before looking at the solutions
Go over the slides and the worksheets we do in class each week (everything is on the course website)
Ask questions in class or in office hours
Consistency pays: do not leave the hard parts for exam week



On reviewing: the worksheets we work in class are the same style as the quiz questions, so going back over them weekly is the cheapest studying there is.
Stress the order: attempt the problem, then read the solution. Reading a worked solution feels like understanding, but working the problem is what produces it.
Push office hours hard. Most students never come, and the ones who do are rarely the ones in trouble.
The honest version: students who struggle are almost never the ones who cannot do it. They are the ones who fall two weeks behind and never catch up.
Ask whether anyone has questions about the syllabus or the course website before moving on.

title: Introduction to the Course
text:
What’s next?

Today: a short diagnostic quiz, ungraded
Before Wednesday: read the syllabus and the course website, and bring questions
Wednesday: why some countries and companies pull ahead, and others do not



Frame Wednesday for this room: the forces that made some countries rich are the same ones that decide which firms grow and which get overtaken. Technology, incentives, and who captures the gains.
That is the backdrop for everything we do later on pricing, costs, and competition.
Hand out the diagnostic with about fifteen minutes left and collect it before students leave.
Remind them it does not count. It exists so I know where to start.
